title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 21: Government of the United States v. Purganan: Extradition and the Right to Bail

primary_topics: Chapter 21 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's account of his ponencia in Government of the United States of America v. Hon. Guillermo G. Purganan, which answered 'in general... No' to two novel questions: whether a prospective extraditee is entitled to notice and hearing before an arrest warrant issues, and whether he is entitled to bail while extradition is pending.

The 'five postulates of extradition' laid down as an essential guide for future cases: extradition as a major instrument for suppressing crime, the presumption that the requesting state will accord due process, the sui generis nature of the proceedings, the duty of good-faith compliance under pacta sunt servanda, and the underlying risk of flight.

The procedure prescribed for trial judges -- study the petition, make a prima facie finding on form and substance, treaty compliance and extraditability, then immediately issue the warrant without notifying the potential extraditee -- and the carefully limited exception allowing bail only on a clear and convincing two-tiered showing.

The Court's sharp internal division, reproduced at length: Justice Carpio's concurrence on reciprocity, the Puno and Bellosillo opinions urging a remand and a higher bail standard, and the Vitug and Santiago dissents accusing the majority of presuming guilt and disregarding basic freedoms -- with CJP's rebuttal that a remand would be 'a cop-out.'
sub_topics: CJP recalls explaining in Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity the two phases of extradition -- an executive evaluation stage and the extradition proper, 'a summary judicial process.'

He recounts Secretary of Justice v. Lantion, where the Court first held 9-6 that an extraditee could see and comment on the documents at the evaluation stage, then reversed itself by the same 9-6 vote after three justices changed their votes.

The facts: Mark Jimenez was the subject of an April 15, 1999 arrest warrant from the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida on indictments for conspiracy to defraud the United States, tax evasion, wire fraud, false statements and illegal campaign contributions, and had fled to the Philippines.

Judge Purganan set the application for an arrest warrant for hearing on June 5, 2001, then on July 3, 2001 ordered the warrant issued while fixing bail at one million pesos in cash, granting Jimenez provisional liberty on July 4, 2001 -- the two Orders the US Government challenged by certiorari.

Postulate one: extradition treaties exist to suppress crime, and with easier international travel extradition has become 'the major effective instrument of international co-operation in the suppression of crime,' deterring flight abroad.

Postulate two: a treaty presupposes that both parties have examined, accept and trust each other's legal system, so our signature signifies confidence that the accused will receive basic rights in the requesting state.

Postulate three: the proceedings are sui generis -- not criminal, summary in nature, with less stringent evidentiary rules and a prima facie standard rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt, and with the President holding final discretion to extradite.

Postulate four: compliance must be in good faith under pacta sunt servanda, since failure 'paints a bad image of our country' and discourages other states from entering treaties that hinge on reciprocity.

Postulate five: extraditees are presumed flight risks, reinforced here by Jimenez's prior acts of leaving the requesting state before his indictment proceedings concluded and remaining here despite knowing his return was sought.

On notice and hearing, the Court read Section 6 of PD 1069: the word 'immediate' qualifies the arrest, the phrase 'if it appears' shows that speed matters more than accuracy at that stage, the word 'hearing' is absent from the warrant provision, and advance notice would give the wanted person 'ample opportunity to escape.'

The Court noted that even the Constitution requires no notice or hearing before a warrant issues in criminal cases, citing Webb v. De Leon, and that Judge Purganan had already made the prima facie finding before gravely abusing his discretion by setting a hearing.

As part of its teaching function the Court outlined the procedure judges must follow on receiving an extradition petition, since the Rules of Court, despite many revisions over a hundred years, contain no provisions governing extraditions.

On bail, the Court held that the constitutional guarantee by its express wording covers only persons arrested for violations of Philippine penal laws; a petition for extradition is 'more akin to a request for police assistance,' and bail should be sought before the courts trying the criminal charges abroad.

On due process, the Court held that its essence is the opportunity to be heard but 'the doctrine does not always call for a prior opportunity'; Jimenez would be fully heard when the extradition petition is heard, and his invocation is hollow since he ran away from the process he already had.

The exception to the no-bail rule: after arrest, bail may be granted only on a clear and convincing showing that the applicant is neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community, and that 'special, humanitarian and compelling circumstances' exist, including reciprocity-based grounds used by the requesting state's highest court.

Because the exception rests on general principles of justice rather than statute, the applicant bears the burden 'with clarity, precision and emphatic forcefulness,' and judicial intrusion into an essentially executive power must be characterized by caution.

Jimenez's claimed special circumstances were rejected: election to Congress after the request was filed (disenfranchisement already debunked in People v. Jalosjos), delay in the proceedings absent bad faith, and the fact that he had not yet fled.

The 10-point summation restating the purpose of extradition, the trust reposed in the treaty partner, the non-criminal character of the proceedings, the judge's prima facie duty, the burden on bail applicants, the sufficiency of subsequent due process, the Court's self-awareness of its limits, executive primacy, and the warning against 'over-due process.'

Justice Carpio concurred that bail is a criminal right unavailable in international extradition, but argued for carefully limited exceptions by reciprocity, and found Jimenez a serious flight risk whose Witness Protection Program claim lacked the operative Certificate of Admission.

Justice Puno, joined by two others, urged a remand: the petition did not establish sufficient factual basis for arrest, 'the doctrine that speed should be preferred to accuracy' breeds recklessness, and the right to bail survives the treaty's silence -- but under a higher, clear-and-convincing standard with the burden shifted to the extraditee.

Justice Bellosillo joined the call for remand, holding that the power to admit to bail is 'a necessary incident of the power to hear and determine cases,' that neither treaty nor PD 1069 withholds it, and that Jimenez's public stature made flight remote, as in Montano v. Ocampo.

Justices Vitug and Ynares-Santiago dissented outright: Vitug on Section 13, Article III and the criticized 'special circumstances' standard of Wright v. Henkel; Santiago on the majority's 'presumption of guilt,' its 'absence of logic' on bail, and her own authorship of People v. Jalosjos, which she distinguished.

CJP's refutation: the parties had been heard through memoranda, position papers and oral arguments, Jimenez himself never asked for a remand, and a remand would only repeat the process -- 'What we need now is prudent and deliberate speed' -- while the charge of disregarding basic freedoms was 'not only baseless, but also unfair.'

stances.claim: A prospective extraditee is not entitled to notice and hearing before a warrant for his arrest issues; the judge need only make a prima facie finding on the petition and must not inform the potential extraditee beforehand, lest he escape.
stances.rhetorical_move: close statutory reading of Section 6 of PD 1069 -- the words 'immediate' and 'if it appears' and the absence of 'hearing' -- backed by constitutional analogy to Webb v. De Leon

stances.claim: Bail is not a matter of right in extradition cases, because the constitutional guarantee by its express wording reaches only persons arrested for violating Philippine penal laws and extradition courts render no judgment of conviction or acquittal.
stances.rhetorical_move: text-and-nature argument: extradition recast as a request for police assistance rather than a criminal prosecution

stances.claim: Persons sought to be extradited are presumed to be flight risks, a presumption reinforced by Jimenez's own prior acts of leaving the United States before his indictment proceedings concluded and staying here despite knowing his return was sought.
stances.rhetorical_move: postulate stated as a general presumption, then validated on the record of the very case at hand

stances.claim: Due process does not always require a prior opportunity to be heard; a subsequent opportunity at the hearing on the extradition petition is enough, and Jimenez's invocation of due process is hollow because he had that opportunity in the requesting state and ran away.
stances.rhetorical_move: flexible-due-process argument closed with a turnabout on the respondent's own conduct

stances.claim: Bail may nonetheless be granted as a carefully limited exception, only on a clear and convincing two-tiered showing of no flight risk and of special, humanitarian and compelling circumstances, with reciprocity as a recognized ground.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-plus-exception construction that concedes fairness while placing a heavy burden on the applicant

stances.claim: Remanding the case would be 'totally unnecessary... a cop-out,' since the parties were exhaustively heard, Jimenez never asked for a remand, and the defect lies not in the factual presentation but in the legal arguments.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-record rebuttal, enumerating the pleadings and oral arguments already had

stances.claim: The right to bail in extradition survives the silence of the treaty and the law, being rooted in due process and supported by international norms, so the case should be remanded for the extradition court to apply a higher and stricter standard.
stances.rhetorical_move: rebalancing-of-competing-interests argument drawn from comparative and treaty sources

notable_anecdotes: CJP notes that in Lantion the Court reversed itself on reconsideration by an identical 9-6 vote after three justices changed their votes -- an unusual detail he records before turning to his own case.

He reports that Judge Purganan inaccurately labelled his prima facie finding 'probable cause,' and that having already found immediate arrest would best serve the ends of justice, the judge then gravely abused his discretion by still setting a hearing.

He observes that the Rules of Court, 'despite being revised many times over during the last one hundred years,' still contain no provisions governing extraditions -- which is why the Court wrote out the procedure as part of its teaching function.

He recounts Justice Carpio's dismantling of Jimenez's Witness Protection Program claim: the DOJ, which administers the program, disowned issuing him a Certificate of Admission, making his state-witness claim 'baseless and self-serving.'

He quotes Justice Bellosillo's memorable framing of his own vote -- that he preferred 'to surf with the reflections of Mr. Justice Puno' -- and Bellosillo's portrait of Jimenez as a man 'whose face is more frequently plastered in the tri-media.'

He records Justice Santiago's rejoinder that the majority cited her own ponencia in People v. Jalosjos against her, and her distinction that Jalosjos had already been convicted while Jimenez 'has not even faced trial yet.'

He notes that the Court heard the parties in Oral Arguments, 'a procedure not normally observed in the great majority of cases in this Tribunal,' and that afterwards the parties 'bombarded' it with Manifestations and a Counter-Manifestation.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' recounts Panganiban's ponencia in Government of the United States of America v. Hon. Guillermo G. Purganan, in which an eight-member majority answered 'in general... No' to two novel questions: whether Mark Jimenez was entitled to notice and hearing before a warrant for his arrest could issue, and whether he was entitled to bail while extradition proceedings were pending. After recalling Secretary of Justice v. Lantion, where the Court reversed itself 9-6 on reconsideration, he narrates how the United States sought Jimenez's extradition on Florida indictments for conspiracy to defraud, tax evasion, wire fraud, false statements and illegal campaign contributions, and how Judge Purganan instead held a hearing, issued the warrant and then fixed bail at one million pesos. The Decision first laid down 'five postulates of extradition': that extradition is a major instrument for the suppression of crime; that the requesting state will accord due process; that the proceedings are sui generis and summary; that compliance must be in good faith under pacta sunt servanda; and that 'persons to be extradited are presumed to be flight risks.' Reading Section 6 of PD 1069, the Court held that the words 'immediate' and 'if it appears' and the absence of 'hearing' dispense with prior notice, and it outlined the procedure judges must follow since the Rules of Court contain none. On bail it held the constitutional guarantee inapplicable, due process satisfied by a subsequent hearing, and bail available only as an exception on a clear and convincing showing of no flight risk and of 'special, humanitarian and compelling circumstances,' including reciprocity. Panganiban then reproduced Carpio's concurrence, the Puno and Bellosillo opinions urging a remand, and the Vitug and Santiago dissents, before rebutting the remand as 'a cop-out' and the charge of disregarding basic freedoms as 'baseless.'
